speaker: Doctor
text: I need to clarify the nature of your wrist pain and skin lesions. On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate the intensity of the pain, and can you describe what the lesions look like? Additionally, when did the fever start compared to the onset of the skin rash?

speaker: Patient
text: 17-year-old male. The patient presents with a 3-day history of pain in his left wrist, which worsened this morning accompanied by chills and malaise. He recounts having a self-resolving left knee pain the previous week. Reports recent return from a camping trip in Minnesota. Sexually active with one female partner. No history of trauma to the wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: CBC with differential, ESR, CRP, and RPR. Did you notice any joint swelling, redness, or warmth in your wrist or knee, and did the rash appear before or after the joint pain? REQUEST IMAGES: Dermatology of wrist lesions and knee.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CBC: WBC 15,000 /μL (elevated), Hemoglobin 14 g/dL, Platelets 300,000 /μL. ESR: Not reported. CRP: Not reported. RPR: Not reported. Joint Examination: Yes, left wrist showed swelling, erythema, and severe tenderness; knee had a history of self-resolving pain. Rash: Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on dorsum of wrists/hands and left palm (note: rash appeared concurrent with current acute symptoms, though history indicates prior joint pain).

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain in the left wrist. I also have Chills, Malaise, Painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands, Swelling and erythema of the left wrist, Severe tenderness to palpation and passive movement of the left wrist. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Iron deficiency anemia and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI). The clinical picture of migratory polyarthralgia, a monoarticular septic wrist, fever, and pathognomonic violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on the extremities, combined with your sexual history, makes this the definitive diagnosis despite the incorrect suggestion of iron deficiency anemia. I will order joint aspiration and blood cultures to confirm the presence of *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.
